items.question: What do you find intellectually interesting about getting models to learn a company's private data?
items.object: Training models to learn a company's private data
items.answer: What about pre-training or even post-training makes it possible for the models to generalize in these magical emergent ways, and controlling that process so that a company has a set of private data? How do we make the models learn that just as well as the models know the capital of France or how to write Python? So, I think it's a really fun problem to think about.
quotes: What about pre-training or even post-training makes it possible for the models to generalize in these magical emergent ways, and controlling that process so that a company has a set of private data? How do we make the models learn that just as well as the models know the capital of France or how to write Python? So, I think it's a really fun problem to think about.

rubrics.text: The response asks what enables emergent generalization during model pre-training or post-training.
The response asks how to make models learn a company's private data as well as they learn familiar public knowledge or skills.

items.question: How do you see Engram's vision of everyone having their own model differing from the frontier AI labs' approach?
items.object: Engram's vision of personalized models versus the frontier labs' training approach
items.answer: I think the worldview that we have is a bit different from the Frontier Lab worldview, where it's like we want one model that's bigger and bigger, that's more and more intelligent across a variety of domains. Instead, how we see it, we kind of imagine this world where everybody has their own model. A lot of the things that people want to learn are either private, like things that will never see the light of day in a post-training data set, or even conflicting, like the way that I want to do the task is different from how another company or another individual wants to. I think a lot of these things we're already seeing are hard to train into the models with the same tools that we have used for decades in machine learning, which is you have really clean supervision, you have ground truth reward signals, and you create a nice environment and train the model to use the tools to better accomplish this coding task. Instead, a lot of the things that actually happen out in the world are very ambiguous, or it's hard to say what makes something good. So I think a lot of these things are very specific to individuals, and very misaligned or not very aligned with how the Frontier Labs think about the whole training pipeline and what kind of models will exist in the longer term.

rubrics.text: The response states that some information people want models to learn will never appear in post-training datasets because it is private.
The response identifies conflicting preferences across individuals or companies about how a model should perform the same task.
The response states that many real-world tasks lack clear criteria for what constitutes good performance.

items.question: Why do you find continual learning such a compelling problem to work on?
items.answer: I think it's obviously one of the grand challenges in AI. I think everybody's talking about it these days because the models are so smart. What else is left? It's, I think, learning at the edges, learning the remainders of what makes these models useful. It's not just about raw intelligence anymore; it's about learning new things. And I think it also feels very fundamental because it kind of goes back to really understanding what makes the model so good. Right now the models kind of incidentally know a lot of things from pre-training, and we don't really understand why. The internet was just this gift granted to us where there's a diverse set of data that contains all of these different examples of coding and writing and all these other things, and it just happened that way. And now, to figure out how to crack this problem of continual learning, it's about figuring out what about pre-training or even post-training makes it possible for the models to generalize in these magical emergent ways and controlling that process so that a company has a set of private data. How do we make the models learn that just as well as the models know the capital of France or how to write Python? So I think it's a really fun problem to think about.
